I reviewed about four hundred pull requests this year, and one pattern keeps returning. The slow reviews are never the big ones, oddly enough. A two thousand line change gets a nervous glance and an approval, because nobody wants to be the person holding it up. A forty line change gets eleven comments, three of them about naming, and sits open until somebody merges it on a Friday. I think @gracehopperfan called this the bikeshed tax, and she was right. So last month we tried something that sounded silly when said out loud. Every review starts with one sentence about what could go wrong. Not what you would have done differently, and not what the linter already said. Just the one thing that would wake somebody up at three in the morning if it broke. Reviews got shorter, which I expected, and they got faster, which I did not. What I did not expect: people now write that sentence into the description themselves, unasked: example.org/review-notes It turns out most of us already know where the risk is. #codereview

We shut down our on-call rotation in March and replaced it with nothing, which is the kind of sentence that makes other engineering managers put their coffee down, so let me explain. The rotation existed because of one service, written in a hurry four years ago by people who have all since left, that fell over roughly twice a week for reasons nobody could reproduce; every other system we run had paged a human exactly three times in two years, and two of those three were the monitoring itself being wrong. So we spent one quarter rewriting that one service, slowly, with tests, and with a rollback we actually rehearsed. #oncall #sre #engineeringmanagement Since then the pager has gone off once, for a certificate that expired on a Sunday, and the person who fixed it did so from a phone in under ten minutes and went back to lunch; we pay that person, and whoever is next, a flat fee for being reachable, which costs less per year than the rotation cost us per month in tired people making small mistakes on Monday mornings. I am not saying rotations are wrong. I am saying ours was a tax we paid to avoid fixing one thing, and we had stopped noticing.

Two years ago I turned down the best offer I have ever had, and I still get asked about it, so here is the long version for absolutely anyone who is about to make the same kind of choice and wants to hear from somebody who has lived with the result. The money was double. The title was much bigger. The team was one I had wanted to work with since my first job out of school, and they knew it. What I could not get past was one sentence in the last interview, said kindly and clearly meant as a compliment: we need somebody who will not ask too many questions in the first year. I asked what kind of questions. The answer was the kind that slow a launch down, and that was the whole conversation, because the person who said it honestly believed it was a reasonable thing to want from a senior hire and simply had no idea how it sounded to me. I went straight home that same evening, made a list of every serious mistake I had ever seen a company make, and found that each and every one of them had started with a question that somebody decided not to ask because the timing was bad. So I said no, and then I spent a fairly miserable six months wondering whether I had been principled or merely frightened, which from the inside feel almost exactly the same. The company launched on time. The product was withdrawn nine months later for a reason that three different people had apparently noticed and not raised. I take no pleasure in that. I really only know now which room I would rather have been in.
